caution: A failure to reproduce is not a finding that the paper is wrong. It may be a failure of the attempt.

attempts.label: DANDI:000044
attempts.paper_title: Diversity in neural firing dynamics supports both rigid and learned hippocampal sequences
attempts.entry_title: Rigid and plastic hippocampal sequences (Grosmark and Buzsaki 2016)
attempts.summary: Some main findings held, some did not, and the central rigid versus plastic cell results could not be tested. Sequence scores during running exceeded those in pre-sleep, and fast-firing cells dominated pre-sleep coactivation. Post-sleep scores did not exceed pre-sleep in the pooled test, although they did in all 8 sessions taken separately. The slow-firing cells' coactivation and replay results did not appear. The rigid and plastic analyses depend on the paper's per-cell significance test, which sits in supplementary methods that were unavailable. Place cells numbered 417 against 491.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Grosmark and Buzsaki (2016) on dandiset 000044, which holds eight sessions of CA1 units, LFP, sleep states and track positions from four rats, each with sleep before and after exploring a novel track. It decodes candidate ripple events with a Bayesian decoder, compares sequence scores across PRE, MAZE and POST, estimates each place cell's contribution to sequences, and relates firing rate and ripple gain to coactivation and replay.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Grosmark and Buzsaki (2016) from dandiset 000044

outcomes.statement: Recordings were made in four rats, in eight novel exploration sessions, each a PRE sleep, a MAZE epoch on one of two linear tracks or a circular track, and a POST sleep.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 2; Figure S1 (as cited in the text)
outcomes.quote: Simultaneous recordings of well-isolated CA1 pyramidal single units were performed in four rats ... exploration of one of two linear or a circular track (MAZE) ... preexperience sleep (PRE) and postexperience sleep (POST) ... (eight novel exploration sessions)
outcomes.notes: 4 subjects and 8 sessions, each with PRE, MAZE and POST epochs in that order (8 of 8), on a 1.6 m linear track (4 sessions), a 2 m linear track (1) and a circular track (3). PRE lasts 2.98 to 5.37 h, MAZE 34.5 to 92.7 min and POST 2.22 to 4.51 h. The rooms the paper names are not in the files.

outcomes.statement: The Bayesian decoder was built from 491 place cells over the eight sessions.
outcomes.quote: a spatial Bayesian decoder (2), constructed from the firing-rate vectors of place cells (n = 491 cells) during track running (eight novel exploration sessions)
outcomes.notes: 417 of the 562 pyramidal units have a smoothed rate-map peak of 1 Hz or more on running, below 491 by more than the tolerance of 49. At 0.5 Hz the count is 480 (within tolerance), at 2 Hz 352, so the count depends strongly on the threshold; the criterion fixes 1 Hz and the other thresholds are variants that do not decide the outcome. By subject, Achilles 181, Buddy 30, Cicero 127, Gatsby 79.
deviations: The place-cell definition is a common choice (peak of 1 Hz or more on running above 5 cm/s, 2 cm bins, 4 cm smoothing); the paper's definition is in the supplementary Methods, which were not available.

outcomes.statement: Sequence scores (rZ) of candidate events are higher in POST sleep than in PRE sleep (replay).
outcomes.quote: Cumulative distribution of rZ for PRE, MAZE, and POSTevents, and 95% confidence intervals. ... Inset, mean ± SE of sequence scores in each condition. *P < 0.05; **P < 0.005; ***P < 0.0005 (Kruskal-Wallis test, followed by post hoc Tukey-Kramer tests).
outcomes.notes: Pooled over sessions, as the criterion fixes the test, POST does not exceed PRE (mean rZ 0.763 against 0.770, Tukey on ranks after Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.412). Within sessions it does; POST is higher in 8 of 8 sessions (sign test p = 0.0039; one-sided rank-sum p < 0.05 in 6), and with each session's PRE mean subtracted POST is higher by 0.106 (p = 2.3e-14). The pooled test is dominated by the three circular-track sessions, which score lower in every epoch (PRE 0.161 and POST 0.260 against 1.112 and 1.207 on the linear tracks, where the event takes the better of two templates) and supply 11161 of 23801 POST events but 5912 of 16448 PRE events. The same test run on each kind of track finds POST above PRE on the five linear-track sessions (Tukey on ranks p = 5.1e-07) and on the three circular-track sessions (p = 1.1e-05). By subject, POST minus PRE is +0.089 (Achilles), +0.185 (Buddy), +0.021 (Cicero) and -0.173 (Gatsby) when pooled within subject.
deviations: Candidate events are population bursts of all units holding a ripple (150 to 250 Hz envelope above 3 SD on one LFP channel per session), outside REM in PRE and POST and below 5 cm/s in MAZE; the paper's detection is in the unavailable Methods.
The rZ null is 200 column-cycle shuffles of the posterior; the paper's shuffle is not stated in the main text.
On the linear tracks each event takes the better of the two direction templates, which raises their scores over those of the single-template circular track.
The Tukey comparison is scipy's Tukey HSD on the pooled ranks, not MATLAB's Tukey-Kramer after kruskalwallis.
Immobility for MAZE candidate events is taken from the 2D head speed, while running for the rate maps is taken from the speed of the linearized position, both at 5 cm/s.

outcomes.statement: Sequence content is higher in MAZE immobility events than in PRE sleep events.
outcomes.quote: the marked increase in sequence content observed in the MAZE and POSTepochs is driven by the recruitment of plastic cells
outcomes.notes: MAZE events score higher than PRE events (mean rZ 1.270 against 0.770, n = 2460 and 16448; Tukey on ranks p printed as 0), and MAZE is higher in all 8 sessions (one-sided rank-sum p from below 0.0001 to 0.0405). It holds on the linear-track sessions (p printed as 0) and on the circular-track sessions (p = 0.0007) separately. MAZE has 76 to 953 scored events per session.
deviations: Events and scores as for fig1c-post-gt-pre.

outcomes.statement: 216 neurons showed significant PCC scores in PRE or POST and were considered to contribute strongly to sequences.
outcomes.quote: Neurons that showed significant PCC scores in either PRE or POST were considered to be strongly contributing to sequence formation (n = 216 neurons (Fig. 2B)
outcomes.notes: The test fixed in the criterion (one-sided signed-rank test of a cell's contributions over its events, p < 0.05) finds 303 strongly contributing cells (72.7% of 417 place cells), against 216. With every rate map shifted it calls 56.1% of cells significant (0.843 on the 1.6 m tracks, 0.905 on the 2 m track, 0.140 on the circular track), so about 234 would be expected by chance. The paper calls these PCC scores significant, which implies a 5% false-positive rate; this test is far from it, so it is not the paper's procedure. The excess is on the linear tracks, where the contribution is taken on the template the event was selected for. A best-template variant of the contribution has a false-positive rate of 0.206 (0.132 in PRE, 0.118 in POST) and finds 188 cells, outside the tolerance; at alpha 0.001 its false-positive rate is 0.031 and it finds 95. The false-positive rates are measured on every fourth PRE and POST event, so on all events they would likely be higher. The best-template numbers are not identical across machines (the verifier's executed copy printed 190 cells and 0.129 in PRE); no conclusion rests on the difference. The PCC definition and its test are in the unavailable Methods.
deviations: The PCC and its significance test are choices made here, as the Methods were not available.
The 20 shifts of a cell's map are drawn afresh for every event.

outcomes.statement: Most neurons strongly contributing to PRE sequences (73%) also contributed to POST sequences.
outcomes.quote: Importantly, the majority of neurons strongly contributing to PRE (73%) also contributed to POST sequences (Fig. 2C and fig. S19)
outcomes.notes: Blocked as it depends on fig2b-strong-contributors. Of 248 PRE strongly contributing cells, 235 (94.8%) also contribute in POST, against a chance level of 69.5%. With the best-template variant 72 of 102 (70.6%), within 73 +/- 7.3, against a chance level of 37.9%.

outcomes.statement: The PRE to POST increase in sequence score is eliminated when the place fields of the 10 to 20% of cells with the highest dPCC are shuffled, and remains after shuffling the bottom 75%.
outcomes.quote: Replay (POST > PRE) was eliminated after shuffling or removal of the top 10 to 20% of cells with the highest ΔPCC scores, whereas it remained after shuffling or removal of the bottom 75%
outcomes.notes: On the pooled test of the criterion replay is absent after shuffling the top 10% (POST minus PRE -0.100, p = 1.0) and the top 20% (-0.127, p = 1.0), but also after shuffling the bottom 75% (+0.022, p = 0.21), so one of the two conditions holds. The pooled test finds no replay before shuffling either (-0.008, p = 0.916), so on all sessions it cannot show a removal. On the five linear-track sessions replay is present before shuffling (+0.101, p < 0.0001), absent after shuffling the top 10% (+0.015, p = 0.23) or 20% (-0.039, p = 0.995) and present after the bottom 75% (+0.098, p < 0.0001); shuffling a random 10% or 20% leaves it (+0.099, +0.088). dPCC is measured on the events that are decoded again. Ranking cells on the even-numbered events and measuring replay on the odd-numbered ones, on the linear tracks replay falls from +0.116 to +0.046 (p = 0.024) after the top 10% and +0.042 (p = 0.038) after the top 20%, so out of sample it is reduced but not removed.
deviations: Variant decodes use 50 column-cycle shuffles per event in place of 200.
dPCC is the difference of the criterion's PCC, whose significance test is not the paper's (fig2b-strong-contributors); the ranking does not use that test.

outcomes.statement: The PRE to POST increase in sequence content is attributable to a small number of plastic cells; removing them, unlike removing rigid cells, removes the increase.
outcomes.quote: The PRE to POST increase in sequence content is attributable to only a small number of plastic cells.
outcomes.notes: Blocked as it depends on fig2b-strong-contributors. On the pooled test, removing plastic cells gives POST minus PRE -0.168 (p = 1.0) and removing rigid cells +0.038 (p = 0.019); removing as many random strongly contributing cells gives -0.023 (p = 0.99). On the linear-track sessions -0.060, +0.136 and +0.094. With classes from the even-numbered events and replay on the odd-numbered ones, the linear tracks give -0.009 (p = 0.54) and +0.090 (p = 0.0027). With the best-template classes, pooled, -0.125 and +0.020 (p = 0.24).

outcomes.statement: Rigid and plastic neurons were similarly distributed along the track.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 3; fig. S2 as cited
outcomes.quote: Rigid and plastic neurons were similarly distributed along the track (fig. S2).
outcomes.notes: Blocked as it depends on fig2b-strong-contributors. Rate-map peaks of rigid and plastic cells do not differ by the KS test (medians 0.419 and 0.486 of the track, D = 0.145, p = 0.072); with the split over all place cells p = 0.079, with the best-template classes p = 0.12.

outcomes.statement: Plastic neurons had higher place-specific indices and fewer place fields than rigid cells.
outcomes.quote: Plastic neurons had higher place-specific indices and fewer place fields compared with rigid cells (Fig. 3A)
outcomes.notes: Blocked as it depends on fig2b-strong-contributors. Plastic cells carry more spatial information (median 0.904 against 0.594 bits per spike, p = 1.9e-05; best-template classes p = 0.0035), but the number of fields does not differ (means 1.484 and 1.685, p = 0.073).

outcomes.statement: Plastic but not rigid neurons increased their spatial specificity (in-field versus out-of-field firing ratio) steadily during the MAZE session.
outcomes.quote: plastic but not rigid neurons increased their spatial specificity steadily during learning (Fig. 3B and fig. S13)
outcomes.notes: Blocked as it depends on fig2b-strong-contributors. Both groups raise their in-field ratio over the session (change of log10 ratio, plastic median 0.155, p = 0.0079; rigid 0.129, p = 0.030; between groups p = 0.41). With the best-template classes plastic p = 0.020 and rigid p = 0.28.

outcomes.statement: Session-wide firing rates of rigid neurons were higher than those of plastic neurons.
outcomes.quote: Session-wide firing rates of rigid neurons were significantly higher compared with plastic neurons (Fig. 4, A and B, and figs. S14 and S15).
outcomes.notes: Blocked as it depends on fig2b-strong-contributors. Rigid cells fire somewhat faster (median 0.700 against 0.591 Hz) without significance (p = 0.062; split over all place cells p = 0.053; best-template classes p = 0.74).

outcomes.statement: Ripple-related spiking, bursting and pairwise coactivation were higher in plastic than in rigid neurons.
outcomes.quote: Ripple-related spiking, bursting, and pair-wise coactivation were higher in plastic versus rigid neurons (Fig. 4A and figs. S14 to S16).
outcomes.notes: Blocked as it depends on fig2b-strong-contributors. Ripple gain (4.489 against 3.939, p = 0.015) and bursting (0.180 against 0.147, p = 0.028) are higher in plastic cells; coactivation is not (0.028 against 0.027, p = 0.90). With the best-template classes none reaches p < 0.05 (gain p = 0.15, bursting p = 0.11).

outcomes.statement: In PRE sleep, coactivation was dominated by fast-firing neurons.
outcomes.quote: In PRE sleep, coactivity was dominated by fast-firing neurons, and these correlations remained unchanged into POST sleep.
outcomes.notes: PRE coactivation rises with firing rate, from 0.0208 in the slowest window to 0.0486 in the fastest; Spearman correlation 0.861 on the averaged curve, positive in 6 of 8 sessions. The POST minus PRE change of the fastest window does not differ from 0 over sessions (sign-rank p = 0.383), which fits the statement that these correlations remain into POST.
deviations: Coactivation over whole epochs, all states; the paper's restriction, if any, is not stated in the main text.

outcomes.statement: Slow-firing neurons showed the strongest increases in coactivation from PRE to POST sleep.
outcomes.quote: In contrast, slow-firing neurons showed the strongest increases in coactivation from PRE to POST sleep (Fig. 4B).
outcomes.notes: The POST minus PRE change does not fall with firing rate; Spearman correlation -0.068 on the averaged curve (p = 0.55), negative in 5 of 8 sessions. The averaged change is 0.0019 in the slowest window and -0.0007 in the fastest, with a maximum of 0.0090.
deviations: Coactivation over whole epochs, all states.

outcomes.statement: Slow-firing cells showed the greatest replay, the partial correlation between RUN and POST coactivation accounting for PRE.
outcomes.quote: Moreover, it was the slow-firing cells that showed the greatest replay (partial correlation across coactivation values between RUN and POST, accounting for PRE).
outcomes.notes: The partial correlation of MAZE running and POST coactivation given PRE is 0.186 in the slowest window and 0.115 in the fastest, but the Spearman correlation over windows is 0.095 and negative in only 4 of 8 sessions. By subject it is -0.588 (Achilles), -0.646 (Buddy), -0.070 (Cicero) and 0.671 (Gatsby).
deviations: MAZE coactivation is taken over running bins (above 5 cm/s on the track).

outcomes.statement: Place cells divided into equal groups by sleep firing rate have medians of 0.39 Hz (low-rate) and 1.12 Hz (high-rate).
outcomes.quote: we divided place cells into equal subgroups by either “off-line” sleep-firing rate or ripple-rate gain ... Low-rate neurons (median, 0.39 Hz) ... than high-rate cells (median, 1.12 Hz)
outcomes.notes: Split by non-REM sleep rate, the low-rate median is 0.435 Hz under both readings, just outside 0.39 +/- 0.039, and the high-rate median 1.091 Hz (a, within sessions) or 1.092 (b, pooled), within 1.12 +/- 0.112. With the rate over all of PRE and POST (a variant) both are within tolerance (0.395 and 1.041 under reading a). The split is of 417 place cells, not 491.
deviations: The paper does not say whether the split is within sessions or pooled; both readings are shown and give the same medians.
Off-line sleep rate is taken as the non-REM rate in PRE and POST; the rate over all of PRE and POST is a variant.

outcomes.statement: Low-rate neurons carried more spatial information per spike on the maze, and increased their within-ripple firing-rate gain from PRE to POST more than high-rate cells.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 6; fig. S16 as cited
outcomes.quote: Low-rate neurons (median, 0.39 Hz) contributed more spatial information per spike on the maze and displayed increased within-ripple firing-rate gains from PRE to POST sleep than high-rate cells
outcomes.notes: Under reading (a), which the criterion selects as neither reading of rate-split-medians matched, low-rate cells carry more spatial information (median 0.975 against 0.622 bits per spike, p = 4.1e-08), but their ripple-gain change from PRE to POST is not larger (0.251 against 0.155, p = 0.948). Reading (b) gives the same.
deviations: Ripple gain is the rate within candidate events over the epoch rate; the paper's definition is in fig. S16, which was not available.

outcomes.statement: Slow-firing, but not fast-firing, neurons increased their contribution to sequences from PRE to POST sleep, in a decoding restricted to each group.
outcomes.quote: Slow-firing, but not fast-firing, neurons increased their contribution to neuronal sequences from PRE to POST sleep (Fig. 4D).
outcomes.notes: On the pooled test neither half shows replay (low-rate POST minus PRE -0.024, p = 0.964; high-rate -0.049, p = 0.9999), as for all cells (-0.008, p = 0.916). In the within-session variant both halves show replay, larger for low-rate cells (+0.116 against +0.058, p of at most 0.0001 for each), which would be the criterion's partial pattern. On the linear-track sessions alone the pooled test also finds both, larger for low-rate cells (+0.077, p = 0.0046, against +0.044, p = 0.018).
deviations: Variant decodes use 50 column-cycle shuffles per event in place of 200.

outcomes.statement: PRE to POST increases in sequence content were limited to cells with high ripple-specific recruitment (gain).
outcomes.quote: Conversely, PRE to POST increases in sequence content were limited to cells that showed a high degree of ripple-specific recruitment (gain) (Fig. 4E and figs. S20 to S22)
outcomes.notes: On the pooled test neither half shows replay (high-gain -0.001, p = 0.71; low-gain -0.111, p = 1.0). In the within-session variant high-gain cells show replay (+0.111, p < 0.0001) and low-gain cells do not (+0.016, p = 0.14), the paper's pattern. On the linear-track sessions alone the pooled test finds replay in neither half (+0.023, p = 0.25; +0.010, p = 0.21) and the within-session variant finds it in both (+0.045, p = 0.029; +0.050, p = 0.0028).
deviations: Gain is the rate within PRE and POST candidate events over the PRE and POST rate, split at the session median.
Variant decodes use 50 column-cycle shuffles per event in place of 200.

findings.statement: In versions 0.210812.1516 and 0.250624.0426 every position series stores its sampling period (0.0256 s) as its rate, so the positions span about 880 to 2360 hours in place of the MAZE epoch. Version 0.261005.2101 stores 39.06 Hz, which matches the epoch lengths.
In Gatsby_08022013 the POST epoch ends at 30413.6 s, while the LFP, the spikes and the sleep states run to about 32000 s.
The dandiset description lists neck EMG and head-mounted accelerometer signals, and the files hold neither; they also hold no wide-band data (acquisition is empty), only the LFP at 1250 Hz.

The paper's derived data are not deposited. There are no candidate or ripple events, no place-cell list, no sequence scores and no PCC values or rigid and plastic labels, so the paper's selections cannot be checked against the dandiset and every one must be rebuilt.

Every electrode's location is "unknown" and no depth or layer is given, so the channel for ripple detection has to be chosen from the signals. Units carry only the hemisphere (lCA1 or rCA1). Subject age is "/".

On the circular track the animals ran toward decreasing linearized position (47 to 63% of samples against 7 to 16% the other way). The series description says the position increases clockwise but not which way the animals ran.

verifications.reviewed: The executed notebook of the first run with the conclusion cells and the summary removed, the helper module and the claims file, with the main text of the paper (the supplement could not be retrieved). The verifier checked the blocked claims against the archive's file list and metadata and tested the helper functions on synthetic inputs. Report in transcripts/000044/verifier-1-report.md.

disagreements.reason: This claim ranks all place cells by dPCC and does not use the strong-contributor selection, so the block reason does not apply (problem 4). By the criterion replay is absent after shuffling the top 10% or 20% but also after shuffling the bottom 75% (p = 0.35); the unmanipulated baseline has no pooled replay either (p = 0.92), so "eliminated" cannot be judged (uninformative). The within-session variant shows the paper's pattern. dPCC is computed from the same PRE and POST events that are decoded again, so the result is circular and there is no control that shuffles a random X% of cells (problem 3).

Replay is absent without plastic cells (p = 1.0) and present without rigid cells (p = 0.020). The result is circular (problem 3), and with the shift-test classes removing rigid cells leaves no replay (p = 0.11).
KS p = 0.034 (cell 37). This is fragile, p = 0.051 under reading (b) and 0.12 under the shift-test variant.
Spatial information is higher in plastic cells (p = 3e-4). The number of fields does not differ (p = 0.52) (cell 39).
Both groups increase: plastic p = 0.015, rigid p = 0.032 (cell 41).
Rigid cells have the higher median, but p = 0.059 (cell 43).
Gain is higher in plastic cells (p = 0.037). Bursting (p = 0.20) and coactivation (p = 0.79) are not (cell 45).

paper_notes.statement: Neither the paper nor the dandiset links analysis code, and the supplementary Materials and Methods, which define the candidate events, place cells, the PCC and its test, are not openly available (PMC and Science serve them only behind a browser check).

attempts.label: DANDI:000044

inputs.what: Synthetic event sequences for the claims on the model (fig4-model-heavy-tails, fig4-model-iet-shapes, model-decremental-equivalent), not deposited by the paper. They are generated in model.ipynb by Algorithms 1 and 2 of the paper's Section IV, implemented in bursttree.py from the pseudocode and Eqs. 9 to 16, with seeds from the claims.

attempts.entry_title: Hierarchical organization of bursty trains in hippocampal spike trains (Hiraoka and Jo 2025)
attempts.summary: In the paper's example hippocampal neuron, burst sizes and merging numbers are heavy-tailed across timescales, and the scaling relation between their exponents holds. The burst-size exponent stays near the paper's 2.35 only above about 130 ms, and the rescaled merging-number distributions narrowly miss collapsing, on a fit setting the paper does not give. Other neurons share the pattern only under a fit poorly suited to integer counts. The Wikipedia and earthquake findings could not be tested, as the edit histories were never deposited and the catalog has no fixed version. In the model, heavy tails held for some timescale series only, and the two algorithms differ because the paper's memory function does not match its merging distribution.
attempts.description: Tests the neuronal findings of Hiraoka and Jo (2025) on dandiset 000044, the hippocampal recordings of Grosmark and Buzsaki (2016) that the paper analyses. It finds the paper's representative unit, measures bursty trains and merging numbers across timescales, fits their power-law tails, and checks whether the other units, pyramidal and inhibitory, show the same pattern. It also runs the paper's two generative algorithms. The Wikipedia and earthquake sequences of the paper are not tested.

outcomes.statement: The representative neuronal sequence (unit 9 of session Achilles-10252013) has 228 356 spikes, with IETs from 1.05 ms to 1.82 x 10^4 ms.
outcomes.source: Section III, paragraph 5; Figure 2, top (Neuronal spikes panel labels)
outcomes.quote: Here, we show the results for a representative event se ... quence for each dataset ... unit 9 in the Achilles-10252013 session in the neuronal spike recordings
outcomes.notes: Under reading (b) of O1, row 9 of the units table of Achilles-10252013 counted from 0 (unit id 18), the unit has 228 356 spikes, tau_min 1.050 ms and tau_max 18 229.7 ms. It is the only unit of the session within all three tolerances. Readings (a) id 9 (9077 spikes), (c) the ninth unit (36 797 spikes) and (d) shank_id 9 (four units) do not match. The unit is labelled inhibitory in this version and interneuron in the latest; the paper describes its neuronal data as pyramidal cells. Its 228 356 spikes are those of the whole session (96 875, 44 099 and 87 382 in the three epochs), which settles O2.

outcomes.statement: The IETs of each process, the representative neuron included, extend across several orders of magnitude.
outcomes.source: Section III, paragraph 6; Figure 2, top left
outcomes.quote: First, the range of IETs in each process extends across several orders of magnitude.
outcomes.notes: tau_max over tau_min is 17 362, 4.24 decades, against the three decades of the criterion; the paper's labels give the same 4.24 decades.

outcomes.statement: For the representative neuron, the burst size distributions are heavy-tailed across different timescales.
outcomes.source: Section III, paragraph 6; Figure 2, top center and legend
outcomes.quote: we con ... firm previous findings that burst size distributions Pδ(b) are heavy-tailed across different timescales
outcomes.notes: With xmin chosen by the KS distance, discrete or continuous, the power law is supported (R > 0, p < 0.05) at 8 of 8 timescales of grid (a) and 40 of 40 of grid (b), all of those below 3000 ms included, with the exponent unbounded or capped at 3. The claim holds under one reading of O3, as the claims file's rule asks. With xmin = 1 the discrete fit is supported at 5 of 8 and 29 of 40, not all below 3000 ms; the continuous fit at 7 of 8 with all 7 below 3000 ms (grid a) and 32 of 40 with 32 of 34 below 3000 ms (grid b). On the IETs shuffled in time, a renewal reference, no timescale is supported under any of the five seeds (0 of 5 or 6, grid (a)).
deviations: The exponent of every fit is unbounded (alpha in [1, inf)), an assumption: the locked powerlaw 2.0.0 caps the power-law alpha at 3 by default (Power_Law.DEFAULT_PARAMETER_RANGES) and its find_xmin discards every candidate xmin whose fit reaches the cap, while the estimator the paper cites (Clauset et al., ref. 36, Section 3) has no upper bound and neither had the package as its paper describes it (Alstott et al., ref. 37; releases 1.x require only alpha > 1). The paper gives no version. The capped fits are run beside the unbounded ones (readings with suffix _cap3).

The grid of delta is open (O4). Grid (b) fits a whole number of log10 steps near 0.052 between the ends of the relevant range (40 steps of 0.0514 for this unit), as the Figure 2 legend says the values shown span the entire range of relevant timescales; every 5th point then gives the delta' labels of Figure 2 and every 8th the delta labels.

outcomes.statement: For neuronal spikes the fitted burst-size exponent stays near 2.35 for several decades of timescales, up to about 3000 ms.
outcomes.source: Section III, paragraph 6; Section III, paragraph 9; Figure 2, top, beta panel
outcomes.quote: our analysis shows that the estimated value of the power ... law exponent fitted to the empirical distribution remains stable for several decades of timescales ... stable around βδ ≃2.35 for neuronal spikes
outcomes.notes: Neither reading of the criterion holds under any fit or grid. Under the discrete KS fit on grid (b) the median beta below 3000 ms is 2.354, inside the band, and 27 of 34 estimates are within 2.35 +/- 0.235, every one from 126.5 ms to 3000 ms (1.4 decades); at 55 ms beta is 3.349, so the range is 1.079 against the 0.47 of reading (b). With the exponent unbounded the ranges are 0.679 to 1.360 over the fits and grids (medians 2.316 to 2.433 under the KS fits, 1.521 to 1.750 with xmin = 1); capped at 3 the KS ranges are 0.552 to 0.705 and also fail. The standard errors are at most 0.088. The paper's value holds from about 130 to 3000 ms but not at the lower end of the relevant range.
deviations: Measured is the median under the discrete KS fit on grid (b); the other readings are in the notebook.

The exponent of every fit is unbounded (alpha in [1, inf)), an assumption: the locked powerlaw 2.0.0 caps the power-law alpha at 3 by default (Power_Law.DEFAULT_PARAMETER_RANGES) and its find_xmin discards every candidate xmin whose fit reaches the cap, while the estimator the paper cites (Clauset et al., ref. 36, Section 3) has no upper bound and neither had the package as its paper describes it (Alstott et al., ref. 37; releases 1.x require only alpha > 1). The paper gives no version. The capped fits are run beside the unbounded ones (readings with suffix _cap3).

outcomes.statement: For neuronal spikes, beta is stable below 3000 ms, where beta at the smaller timescale is below gamma. Above 3000 ms beta decreases, apparently driven by a decreasing gamma.
outcomes.source: Section III, paragraph 9; Figure 2, top, beta and gamma panels
outcomes.quote: for the range of δ < 3000 ms, for which we observe βδ′ < γδδ′. For δ > 3000 ms, the decreasing tendency of βδ seems to be driven by the decreasing γδδ′
outcomes.notes: On grid (b), under both KS fits with the exponent unbounded, beta at delta' is below gamma for 40 of 57 pairs with delta < 3000 ms (38 for the capped continuous fit); above 3000 ms the 6 grid points give a Spearman rho of -0.829 (p = 0.042) for beta, which falls from 2.064 to 1.867 (discrete), and gamma falls with delta for each ratio (rho -0.714, -0.964 and -0.943). Part (2) rests on 6 points at p = 0.042. Grid (a) has one point above 3000 ms, so parts (2) and (3) are not judged on it; its part (1) holds (7 of 12). Under xmin = 1 part (1) fails (24 of 57), so the outcome rests on the KS fits, as O3 allows for a claim on exponents. The paper names no test; the claim's "seems to be driven" is not tested beyond these correlations.

outcomes.statement: For the representative neuron, the merging-number distributions are heavy-tailed for various pairs of timescales, and their fitted exponents gamma stay fairly constant across a wide range of timescales.
outcomes.source: Section III, paragraph 6; Figure 2, top right and gamma panel
outcomes.quote: the merging number distributions Pδδ′(k) also ... heavy tails for various timescale pairs ... although the estimated exponents are not as stable as in burst size distribution, they remain relatively constant across a wide range of timescales
outcomes.notes: With the exponent unbounded, the discrete KS fit supports the power law for 13 of 15 pairs on grid (a) and 70 of 76 on grid (b), and the gamma of the supported pairs has an interquartile range of 0.378 and 0.415 (median 2.618 and 2.644), so both conditions hold under that reading of O3. The continuous KS fit supports 15 of 15 and 69 of 76, but its interquartile range is 0.642 and 0.546; capped at 3 it was 0.408 and 0.426, so the cap decides that reading and not the discrete one (0.383 and 0.401 capped). With xmin = 1 the discrete fit is supported for 6 of 15 and 19 of 76 pairs, and the continuous fit has an interquartile range of 0.673 and 0.597.
deviations: The exponent of every fit is unbounded (alpha in [1, inf)), an assumption: the locked powerlaw 2.0.0 caps the power-law alpha at 3 by default (Power_Law.DEFAULT_PARAMETER_RANGES) and its find_xmin discards every candidate xmin whose fit reaches the cap, while the estimator the paper cites (Clauset et al., ref. 36, Section 3) has no upper bound and neither had the package as its paper describes it (Alstott et al., ref. 37; releases 1.x require only alpha > 1). The paper gives no version. The capped fits are run beside the unbounded ones (readings with suffix _cap3).

outcomes.statement: Rescaled merging-number distributions for different pairs of delta and delta' collapse onto each other, so the burst tree is self-similar across levels.
outcomes.source: Section III, paragraph 6; Figure 2, top right
outcomes.quote: the rescaled distributions for different pairs of δ and δ′ collapse on top of each other, implying that the structure of the burst tree is self-similar across hierarchical levels or timescales
outcomes.notes: Reading (b) fails with the exponent unbounded: the gamma of the 15 pairs of Figure 2 lie up to 0.538 from their median under the discrete KS fit (median 2.610), 1.742 under the continuous KS fit, 0.521 under the discrete fit from xmin = 1 and 1.249 under the continuous one, all outside the band of 0.5. The deviation of 0.538 is the pair delta' 180 ms, delta 594 ms (gamma 3.148), which the cap at 3 holds at 2.843; the capped discrete KS fit, at 0.490, is the only fit within the band, so the outcome rests on the unbounded exponent. Reading (a) fails, as the complementary cumulative distributions of k over its mean differ by up to a factor of 12.54 (median 1.63) where all exceed 10^-3. One pair of Figure 2 (delta' 590 ms, delta 6490 ms) lies above the relevant range, with 89 bursts. The margin is small (0.538 unbounded and 0.490 capped, against 0.5). O3 (a) names the package's default, which in the locked powerlaw 2.0.0 is the capped fit, and read that way the claim would be reproduced; the verifier reads the outcome as undetermined between the two. The unbounded exponent is kept, as the method the paper cites has no cap and the cap clips the estimate that decides the band, and whether the paper's fits were capped is asked of the authors (findings).
deviations: The pairs are the labels of Figure 2 as printed (55, 100, 180, 330 and 590 ms), as the criterion gives them. The comparison points for reading (a) are 200 values of k over its mean, log-spaced from 0.01 to 1000, a standard choice.

The exponent of every fit is unbounded (alpha in [1, inf)), an assumption: the locked powerlaw 2.0.0 caps the power-law alpha at 3 by default (Power_Law.DEFAULT_PARAMETER_RANGES) and its find_xmin discards every candidate xmin whose fit reaches the cap, while the estimator the paper cites (Clauset et al., ref. 36, Section 3) has no upper bound and neither had the package as its paper describes it (Alstott et al., ref. 37; releases 1.x require only alpha > 1). The paper gives no version. The capped fits are run beside the unbounded ones (readings with suffix _cap3).

outcomes.statement: In most cases both gamma and the burst-size exponent at the smaller timescale exceed 2, so the scaling relation reduces to beta at delta equal to the smaller of gamma and beta at delta', which agrees with the observations.
outcomes.source: Section III, paragraphs 8 and 9 (Eqs. 7 and 8); Figure 2
outcomes.quote: Since γδδ′, βδ′ > 2 in most cases as shown in Fig. 2, we have
outcomes.notes: Under the KS fits with the exponent unbounded both gamma and beta at delta' exceed 2 in 15 of 15 pairs (grid a) and 76 of 76 (grid b), and beta at delta is within 10% of the smaller of the two in 9 (continuous) and 12 (discrete) of 15 and in 45 and 58 of 76 pairs (median relative error 0.058 to 0.089); capped at 3, in 11 and 12 of 15 and 48 and 58 of 76. Under xmin = 1 both conditions fail (both above 2 in 0 to 17 pairs).

outcomes.statement: Other neurons of the recordings show patterns similar to the representative unit, with heavy-tailed burst-size and merging-number distributions across timescales.
outcomes.quote: Other sequences in the datasets show similar patterns.
outcomes.notes: Reproduced under the continuous fit from xmin = 1 alone, which meets the criterion's "under one reading": with the exponent unbounded, 502 of 554 (grid a) and 502 of 562 (grid b) pyramidal units of all sessions show the pattern (0.906 and 0.893), and 107 and 106 of 120 in Achilles-10252013 (0.892 and 0.883). No other reading meets it: in set (b) the continuous KS fit gives 0.449 and 0.454, the discrete KS fit 0.233 and 0.240, the discrete fit from xmin = 1 0.211 and 0.215; in set (a) 0.342 and 0.292, 0.117 and 0.083, and 0.017. The pass is fragile: the continuous fit from xmin = 1 treats integer sizes as continuous down to 1, where Clauset et al. (ref. 36) find the continuous approximation poor, and its exponents (median over units of the median beta 1.744 to 1.778) are far from the paper's 2.35. Capped at 3 (other_neurons_cap3.ipynb, grid a) the continuous KS fit passes in set (b) (0.547) and the continuous fit from xmin = 1 gives 0.906, so the outcome does not depend on the cap. The inhibitory units, the class the files give the paper's representative unit, show the pattern far more often under the KS fits: 92 and 87 of 128 (0.719 and 0.680, discrete) and 95 of 128 (0.742, continuous); over all 690 units the continuous KS fit gives 0.504 and 0.507. Under the discrete KS fit the median over pyramidal units of each unit's median beta is 2.471 and 2.459 (interquartile range 2.216 to 2.789, grid a), and 2.284 to 2.600 by session; the burst-size part holds in 0.744 and 0.770 of the units and the merging-number part in 0.251 and 0.249. 32 pyramidal units have fewer than three points on grid (a) and are not used there. Whether the set should hold the inhibitory units is asked of a reader (questions).
deviations: Pyramidal units are read as those with cell_type excitatory, the only label for principal cells in this version (562 of 690 units). The paper's own representative unit is labelled inhibitory, so the inhibitory units (128) and all units (690) are run as variants.
Two of the 562 pyramidal units have unsorted spike times (data finding); the trains are sorted before the IETs are taken, and leaving them out changes no fraction by more than 0.003.

The exponent of every fit is unbounded (alpha in [1, inf)), an assumption: the locked powerlaw 2.0.0 caps the power-law alpha at 3 by default (Power_Law.DEFAULT_PARAMETER_RANGES) and its find_xmin discards every candidate xmin whose fit reaches the cap, while the estimator the paper cites (Clauset et al., ref. 36, Section 3) has no upper bound and neither had the package as its paper describes it (Alstott et al., ref. 37; releases 1.x require only alpha > 1). The paper gives no version. The capped fits are run beside the unbounded ones (readings with suffix _cap3). The capped variant is run on grid (a) alone, for run time.

outcomes.statement: For the most frequent Wikipedia editor (n = 1 154 494 edits), the burst-size exponent is stable around 2.50, and the merging-number distributions are heavy-tailed.
outcomes.source: Section III, paragraphs 3 and 6; Figure 2, middle
outcomes.quote: βδ ≃2.50 for Wikipedia edits
outcomes.notes: The paper's preprocessed edit histories were provided privately and are not deposited. The English Wikipedia dump of October 2, 2015 is no longer on dumps.wikimedia.org (the directory answers 404) but is kept on the Internet Archive (item enwiki-20151002), where the smallest file holding every revision's editor and time, the stub-meta-history, is 47.4 GB compressed. Streaming and parsing it to rebuild the editors' sequences, with a preprocessing and a definition of frequent editors the paper does not give, does not fit the run's time. The verifier would give data_missing, as the preprocessed edit histories were never deposited; the code stays too_large, as the claims file has this claim as data elsewhere, for which the protocol does not use data_missing, and the public dump it would be rebuilt from is what does not fit the run.
outcomes.where: Preprocessed edit histories derived from the English Wikipedia dump of October 2, 2015 (https://dumps.wikimedia.org/; refs. 26, 40 and 41), provided to the authors by Woo-Sik Son; not deposited

outcomes.statement: For earthquakes in the south cluster of Southern California (n = 330 215 events, 1993 to 2020), the burst-size exponent is stable around 2.60, and the merging-number distributions are heavy-tailed.
outcomes.source: Section III, paragraphs 4 and 6; Figure 2, bottom
outcomes.quote: βδ ≃2.60 for earthquakes
outcomes.notes: The Southern California Seismic Network catalog is public (the SCEDC event service answered a query for 1993) but it is revised continuously and has no versioned release, and the paper gives no retrieval date or event identifiers, so it cannot be pinned as the protocol requires for outside data (author, step 1.4). Not tested. The verifier finds this reason weak, since the 10% tolerance on n would allow an approximate test on the current catalog; such a test would rest on unpinned data and was not run.
outcomes.where: Southern California Seismic Network catalog (FDSN network CI, https://www.fdsn.org/networks/detail/CI/), events January 1, 1993 to December 31, 2020, clustered by DBSCAN with eps 0.07 degrees and 35 minimum points

outcomes.statement: Event sequences generated by the incremental dynamic algorithm, with linear, quadratic or exponential timescale series, show heavy-tailed burst-size and merging-number distributions over a wide range of timescales, with stable exponents.
outcomes.quote: For all of the three timescale series, the generated ... show heavy-tailed distributions of burst sizes b for a wide range of timescales δ ... numbers k are also heavy-tailed across different pairs of timescales δ and δ′, even though these timescales do not coincide with the preset series of timescales δl ... the power-law exponent values of the heavy tails in Pδ(b) and Pδδ′(k) are stable across timescales
outcomes.notes: Sequences generated here by Algorithm 2 with the set-up of Section IV. With the exponent unbounded, no single reading of the fit holds for all three series under the claim's seed, on either grid. Under the discrete KS fit the linear and quadratic series hold on grid (a); the exponential series has heavy tails (supported at 8 of 11 timescales and 17 of 20 pairs on grid a, 42 of 52 and 79 of 94 on grid b) but its gamma has an interquartile range of 0.544 and 0.508, above the 0.5 of the criterion, and on grid (b) the linear series also fails (0.511). The fits from xmin = 1 hold for the exponential series but not the quadratic one (beta interquartile range 0.508 to 0.953). Capped at 3 (grid a), the discrete KS fit gives 0.522 for the exponential gamma. Under the four further seeds the discrete KS fit holds for all three series under seeds + 1000, + 2000 and + 3000 and not under + 4000 (the linear series fails); the exponential gamma interquartile range runs from 0.203 to 0.544 over the five seeds. Each series holds under some reading under every seed on grid (a). The criterion defines no partial outcome; partially reproduced is the protocol's outcome for a result that holds only in part, and the criterion holds for two of its three series under the adopted reading. This differs from fig2-neuron-beta-stable, which is not reproduced because no reading meets its single condition.
deviations: One reading of the fit is applied to all three series alike, the adopted discrete KS fit; taking for each series whichever reading holds would give reproduced.
Under the four further seeds only grid (a) was run, with the exponent unbounded, for run time.
No code is linked for Algorithm 2; it is implemented from the pseudocode and Section IV (Eqs. 10, 12 to 14 and 16).

The exponent of every fit is unbounded (alpha in [1, inf)), an assumption: the locked powerlaw 2.0.0 caps the power-law alpha at 3 by default (Power_Law.DEFAULT_PARAMETER_RANGES) and its find_xmin discards every candidate xmin whose fit reaches the cap, while the estimator the paper cites (Clauset et al., ref. 36, Section 3) has no upper bound and neither had the package as its paper describes it (Alstott et al., ref. 37; releases 1.x require only alpha > 1). The paper gives no version. The capped fits are run beside the unbounded ones (readings with suffix _cap3). The capped fits are run under the claim's seed on grid (a).
outcomes.where: Not deposited; generated by the paper's Algorithm 2 (Section IV), for which no code is linked

outcomes.statement: The IET distribution of the model depends on the timescale series. With linear timescales it resembles that of the earthquakes, and with exponential timescales it is a power law reminiscent of the Wikipedia edits.
outcomes.source: Section IV, paragraph 11; Figure 4, left column, and Figure 2, left column
outcomes.quote: generated using a linear timescale series has a similar shape to that for the earthquake sequence, while the power-law IET distribution for the sequence based on the exponential timescales is reminiscent of that for the data on Wikipedia edits
outcomes.notes: Under the claim's seed tau_max is 1711.4 (linear, 0.127 below 1960), 21 390.9 (quadratic, within 10% of 20 800) and 61 320.3 (exponential, 0.249 below 81 600), so one of three is within tolerance. tau_max is an IET of the highest level the sequence reaches, which varies with the seed (levels 14 to 18 linear, 14 to 16 quadratic and 13 to 18 exponential, against 19, 14 and 16 for the paper's values); over the five seeds the values are within 10% in 2, 2 and 0 of 5. tau_min is 1.000 or 1.001 throughout, as in Figure 4. The comparison of shapes with the earthquake and Wikipedia sequences is not judged and cannot be made here; the model's P(tau) falls with log-log slopes of -2.27, -1.98 and -2.15 above tau = 10. The criterion defines no partial outcome; partially reproduced is used, as the protocol defines it, because one of the three expected values is within its tolerance and two are not.
outcomes.where: Not deposited; generated by the paper's Algorithm 2 (Section IV), and the Wikipedia and earthquake data named in fig2-wikipedia-beta and fig2-earthquake-beta

outcomes.statement: The decremental algorithm (Algorithm 1) produces sequences statistically equivalent to those of the incremental algorithm (Algorithm 2), since the memory function of Eq. 9 encodes the whole merging-number distribution.
outcomes.quote: We omit the results for event sequences generated by the decremental algorithm since it produces statistically equivalent sequences as the incremental one.
outcomes.notes: Under the literal set-up of Section IV (Algorithm 1 with the zeta distribution of Eq. 15, Algorithm 2 with the memory function of Eq. 16) the burst sizes differ at every relevant timescale of the three series under the claim's seed (23 of 23 on grid a, 113 of 113 on grid b; 22 to 25 and 105 to 114 over the five seeds), with KS D up to 0.4487, and the decremental sequence has more bursts at the lowest timescale (566 721 against 414 726, linear). Eq. 16 is not the memory function Eq. 9 gives for the zeta distribution (q(1) is 0.354 against 0.255; mean merging number 2.59 against 1.93). With both algorithms on one distribution (readings Z and Q) the differences are small (D at most 0.1874), but the criterion still rejects at 3 and 11 (Z) and 4 and 11 (Q) timescales under the claim's seed, as it does for two runs of the same algorithm (reference N, 4 and 11), so the KS criterion rejects even identical algorithms on these correlated sequences. Every reading is not reproduced under the claim's seed; reading Z passes under seed + 4000 (0 and 0 rejections), hence seed_sensitive. The literal reading is not reproduced under all five seeds. As a variant the verifier asked for, a test calibrated across runs takes the five runs of each algorithm as the units (mean KS distance between algorithms less within, averaged over grid (a), exact permutation over the 126 splits): L differs in all three series (p = 0.0079, the smallest possible, 0.024 after Bonferroni), two runs of one algorithm (N) differ in none (p 0.373 to 0.913), Z in none (p 0.429 to 0.857), and Q in the linear series only (p = 0.0079). It agrees with the criterion on L and finds the algorithms equivalent under Z; it does not decide the outcome. Whether the criterion's test can decide equivalence, since it rejects two runs of one algorithm, is asked of a reader (questions); the outcome stands under the calibrated test as well, as L differs there in all three series.
deviations: The paper's "statistically equivalent" holds by construction when the decremental algorithm draws from the distribution whose memory function the incremental one uses. The three readings of the set-up (L literal, Z both zeta, Q both from Eq. 16) are all run, with two runs of Algorithm 2 as the reference of the test.
The relevant timescales of each comparison are those of the incremental sequence.
outcomes.where: Not deposited; generated by the paper's Algorithms 1 and 2 (Section IV)

findings.statement: In Buddy-06272013, Cicero-09012014 and Gatsby-08022013 the spike train of unit id 2 is not sorted in time. Each is two sorted runs, the first of exactly 65 536 spikes (131 072 in Gatsby-08022013) starting in mid-session and running to the end of the recording, the second starting near the session's start. The power-of-two length suggests a fault in the conversion; whether the train holds one unit's spikes could not be told.
In Gatsby-08022013, 263 976 spikes (4.7%) fall after the end of the last epoch (30 413.6 s), up to 32 002.4 s, in no epoch.

The position series of the maze stores its sampling interval (0.0256 s) in the attribute rate of starting_time, which NWB defines in Hz. Read as a rate the series would last 3 154 777 s; read as an interval it lasts the 2067.5 s of the maze epoch.

The units table ids of the cited version (id 18 for the paper's "unit 9") differ from those of the latest version (id 119 for the same row, with a cluster_id of 19), and neither holds the number the paper uses. The paper's unit can be found only as a row position, and only because its spike count and IETs match the paper's figure.

No spike train is deposited twice (no two units share their spike count and first and last spike, within or across the eight sessions), and the spikes and the maze position share a clock (the excitatory population rate correlates with running speed at r = 0.618 at zero shift and at a median absolute r of 0.043 beyond 60 s). The epochs differ from the paper's description of 45 minutes of maze and four hours of rest each, with maze epochs of 0.57 to 1.54 h and first rest periods of 2.98 to 5.37 h.

The verifier also queried the DANDI API for the dandiset's assets and ran powerlaw 2.0.0 on synthetic zeta samples.

disagreements.reason: Neither reading holds under any fit reading or grid. For example, ks_discrete on grid b has median 2.354, which is in the band, but its range is 0.705 against < 0.47 allowed. Beta is 2.6 to 2.9 for delta below about 130 to 180 ms, and only from 126 to 183 ms to 3000 ms (about 1.2 decades) do all estimates sit within 2.35 +/- 0.235. Removing the cap in problem 1 would only widen the range.

Support is robust, 15/15 (ks_continuous, grid a) and 72/76 (grid b). The IQR condition (0.38 to 0.43 against < 0.5) depends on an estimator that is bounded at alpha < 3 (problem 1). Six of the 15 grid-(a) gamma values sit at 2.93 to 2.99, which is that bound. Without the cap the IQR would very likely exceed 0.5, so only the first condition is secure.

Reproduced (fragile). The criterion is met under one reading. In set (b), ks_continuous gives 0.547 (grid a) and 0.560 (grid b), and x1_continuous gives 0.89 to 0.91. Set (a) passes only under x1_continuous (0.89). ks_discrete, the natural fit for integer data, gives 0.08 to 0.23. The set itself is questionable (problem 2).

paper_notes.statement: The paper describes its neuronal data as recordings of pyramidal cells, but its representative unit (row 9 of Achilles-10252013) is labelled inhibitory in the cited version and interneuron in the latest. Which units the paper analysed, and whether it used the cell types, is not said. Under the KS fits the inhibitory units show the paper's pattern far more often than the pyramidal ones (0.68 to 0.74 of 128 against 0.23 to 0.45 of 562; in Achilles-10252013 alone 0.76 to 0.88 of 17 against 0.08 to 0.34 of 120).

Section IV gives the zeta distribution (Eq. 15) as P(k) and calls Eq. 16 the memory function that Eq. 9 gives for it, but Eq. 9 applied to the zeta distribution gives q(1) = 0.255, not the 0.354 of Eq. 16. The incremental algorithm with Eq. 16 therefore draws merging numbers with P(K >= k) = k^-(gamma-1) (mean 2.59), and the decremental one with Eq. 15 draws zeta numbers (mean 1.93), so the two are not statistically equivalent as set up.

Question for the authors. Which power-law fit was used for burst sizes and merging numbers, discrete or continuous, and with xmin chosen by the KS distance or fixed? The paper cites Clauset et al. and the powerlaw package without its options or version. On this dataset the discrete fit with xmin by the KS distance gives the paper's beta of 2.35 for unit 9, and the choice decides whether other neurons show the pattern (23% of pyramidal units under it, 45% under the package's continuous default with xmin by the KS distance, 89% to 91% with the continuous fit from xmin = 1).

Question for the authors. Which grid of timescales was used, and which units were meant by "other sequences in the datasets"? The Figure 2 labels fit a log-spaced grid of 40 steps of 0.0514 over the relevant range; this attempt used its 40 points below the upper end (55.2 to 5581.5 ms), since the upper end has fewer than 100 bursts. Whether all units or the pyramidal ones were analysed is not said. Which merging-number distribution did the decremental algorithm draw from, given that Eq. 16 is not the memory function of the zeta distribution?

Question for the authors. Which release of powerlaw was used, and was the exponent bounded? Release 2.0.0 caps the power-law exponent at 3 by default and lets the cap move the KS choice of xmin; the method of Clauset et al. that the paper cites has no cap. On the representative unit the cap decides the collapse of the merging-number exponents (largest deviation from the median 0.490 capped, 0.538 unbounded, against a band of 0.5) and narrows the spread of beta at the smallest timescales (2.907 capped, 3.349 unbounded at 55 ms). This attempt assumed an unbounded exponent.

entries.name: grosmark-2016-000044
entries.title: Rigid and plastic hippocampal sequences (Grosmark and Buzsaki 2016)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Grosmark and Buzsaki (2016) on dandiset 000044, which holds eight sessions of CA1 units, LFP, sleep states and track positions from four rats, each with sleep before and after exploring a novel track. It decodes candidate ripple events with a Bayesian decoder, compares sequence scores across PRE, MAZE and POST, estimates each place cell's contribution to sequences, and relates firing rate and ripple gain to coactivation and replay.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Grosmark and Buzsaki (2016) from dandiset 000044

entries.name: hiraoka-2025
entries.title: Hierarchical organization of bursty trains in hippocampal spike trains (Hiraoka and Jo 2025)
entries.description: Tests the neuronal findings of Hiraoka and Jo (2025) on dandiset 000044, the hippocampal recordings of Grosmark and Buzsaki (2016) that the paper analyses. It finds the paper's representative unit, measures bursty trains and merging numbers across timescales, fits their power-law tails, and checks whether the other units, pyramidal and inhibitory, show the same pattern. It also runs the paper's two generative algorithms. The Wikipedia and earthquake sequences of the paper are not tested.
